column5: Yusuf brothers' bloodied robe; visual testimony
column6: The commentary quotes the brothers anticipating that Yaqub will not believe them; Genesis has them present Joseph's bloodied robe and ask their father to identify it. Both stage a claim through an object offered for inspection.

In the commentary's Qur'anic scene Yaqub rejects the brothers' account as something their souls invented; Genesis has him infer from the robe that Joseph was devoured. The changed response to misleading evidence is the point.

The commentary quotes the brothers saying their father would not believe them even if truthful; in Genesis they report Joseph is alive and Jacob does not believe them. The shared family scene turns on whether a report is credible.

The commentary permits a reading in which seeing precedes confirmation; Genesis says Jacob's spirit revives when he sees the wagons Joseph sent. Here visible evidence changes his response to the report.

The commentary quotes Musa saying he saw a fire and may bring back a coal or find guidance; Exodus has Moses see the angel of the LORD in a flame within a bush. The shared encounter presents fire as a visible sign, while the Qur'anic gloss stresses wayfinding.
The commentary develops seeing as noticing and examining; Moses turns aside to see why the bush is not consumed. The biblical scene makes looking an inquiry rather than mere sight.

The commentary's Yusuf example makes credibility the issue; Moses tells the LORD that Israel will not believe him or listen to his voice. This is a distinct biblical scene where a messenger worries that his report will not be accepted.

The commentary glosses iman as tasdiq; after giving Moses signs, the LORD says they are meant so Israel may believe that the God of their ancestors appeared to him. The signs explicitly connect visible evidence with assent.
The commentary connects seeing with becoming sure; Exodus distinguishes a sign that may fail to persuade from a second sign that may be believed. It gives a staged test of a messenger's claim.

The commentary says the sequence may be read as seeing and then confirming, though the narrative alone does not require it; Israel sees the great act at the sea, fears the LORD, and believes in him and Moses. This is an explicit biblical sequence of sight and belief.

column5: words verified by a required check
column6: The commentary quotes confirmation of a saying; Joseph makes the brothers bring Benjamin so their claim can be tested and they will not die. This is a narrative case where corroboration is demanded before a report is accepted.

The commentary joins iman and haqq as the soul's assent to truth; Genesis says Abram believed YHWH and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. The verse links belief with right standing in a concrete promise scene.

The commentary describes people who see and pass confirmed truth to one another; Deuteronomy tells Israel not to forget what their eyes saw and to teach it to children and grandchildren. Sight becomes communal transmission across generations.

The commentary's exception joins belief to righteous deeds; Deuteronomy says doing the commandments carefully will be righteousness for Israel. This gives a Torah formulation in which right standing is tied to practice.

The commentary treats belief as confirmation and cites checking a report; Deuteronomy says not to follow a prophet whose sign succeeds if he urges other gods, because God is testing Israel's love. A striking sign alone does not establish a trustworthy message.

The commentary's haqq includes verifying an affair and becoming certain; Deuteronomy says a failed prediction shows that the word was not spoken by the LORD. It gives a specific test for a claim of divine speech.

The commentary contrasts truthful counsel with a report that needs checking; Exodus forbids carrying a false report or joining a malicious witness. The law guards the circulation of claims among a community.

The commentary's Yusuf scene concerns whether to accept a claim; Proverbs says the simple believe every word while the prudent consider their steps. It directly distinguishes credulity from discernment.

column5: the second account tests the first
column6: The commentary links certainty to checking what one is told; Proverbs says the first litigant seems right until another comes and examines him. It makes cross-examination the means by which an initially plausible account is tested.

The commentary's haqq is verified truth passed between people; Proverbs contrasts one who speaks faithfully and declares what is right with a false witness who speaks deceit. The setting is testimony, not an abstract use of truth.

The commentary pairs hearing a report with seeing and confirming; the psalm says what the community heard it has now seen in the city of God. It is a compact communal formula for confirmed experience.

The commentary pairs belief with righteous deeds; Habakkuk says the righteous live by faithfulness. The verse places righteousness and emunah together while leaving open whether the emphasis is trust or fidelity.

The commentary moves from seeing or hearing to affirming what was reported; Luke says his account was handed down by eyewitnesses and servants of the word. The verse connects sensory witness with transmitted teaching.

The commentary glosses haqq as verifying an affair and becoming certain; Luke says he writes so Theophilus may know the certainty of what he was taught. This is an explicit account of checked transmission.

The commentary links hearing with confirmation; the Bereans receive Paul's message eagerly and examine the scriptures daily to see whether his claims are so. The scene models welcome joined to verification.

The commentary begins with a person noticing by sight or hearing; First John grounds its proclamation in what the witnesses heard, saw with their eyes, and touched. The sensory sequence supports a claim passed on to others.

The commentary reads tawasaw as people communicating what they have confirmed to each other; First John proclaims what was seen and heard so its audience may share fellowship. It joins testimony to a community formed by receiving it.
The commentary describes confirming an affair and finding it sound; Paul tells the community to test everything and hold fast to what is good. The language directly joins testing with discernment.

The commentary cites checking a report before accepting it; First John says not to believe every spirit but to test the spirits to see whether they are from God. It applies verification to religious claims.
The commentary's exception names both belief and righteous deeds; James says faith without works is dead. The verse makes action a condition of living faith.
The commentary pairs belief with righteous deeds; James points to Abraham offering Isaac as an act by which he was justified. It gives a specific scriptural example of conduct accompanying faith.

The commentary's lexicon glosses iman as confirmation and amal as work; James says Abraham's faith was working with his works and completed by them. This directly joins the two terms' ethical functions.
The commentary joins belief and haqq; James cites Abraham's belief being counted as righteousness and says scripture was fulfilled. It reads the belief as realized through the action just described.
The commentary's exception states belief and deeds together; James concludes that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. This is the clearest Christian formula matching that pairing.
The commentary places iman beside righteous action; Paul says what counts is faith working through love. The verse joins belief to an active ethical expression.

column5: stirring one another toward good works
column6: The commentary reads mutual exhortation in haqq as reciprocal transmission; Hebrews tells readers to consider one another and provoke love and good works. It supplies a concrete communal form of counsel.
The commentary pairs mutual counsel with patience; Hebrews tells the community to encourage one another as the day approaches. The counsel sustains a group through waiting.
The commentary says verified truth is conveyed reciprocally; Hebrews commands daily encouragement so no one is hardened by sin's deceit. It gives mutual counsel an explicit protective purpose.

The commentary reads tawasaw bil-haqq as mutual transmission of truth; Ephesians tells members of one body to put away falsehood and speak truth to each other. The verse makes truthful speech a communal obligation.

The commentary allows loss to be read as a failure of seeing and the exception as return through confirmation; James describes someone wandering from the truth and another bringing him back. It makes communal correction a response to deviation.

The commentary says the people who exhort one another pass confirmed truth; James says the one who brings a sinner back saves that person's soul from death. It gives correction a specific salvific consequence.

The commentary's final pair is reciprocal counsel and patience; Paul tells the community to admonish the disorderly, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with all. The verse combines distinct forms of counsel with sabr-like endurance.
The commentary joins truth with righteous action; the Didache says a prophet is to be assessed by whether conduct matches teaching. It makes deeds a concrete test of a religious claim.

Genesis says Jacob mourns Joseph for many days; the commentary quotes the Qur'anic answer, beautiful patience. The two tellings give distinct responses to the same reported loss without making Genesis deny patience.

The commentary links seeing with confirming what one has been told; after the wagons arrive, Jacob declares that Joseph is alive and says he will go see him. The verse gives the explicit affirmation following the evidence.

column5: ء م ن / אמנ; table sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary glosses haqq as confirming a saying; Joseph tells his brothers their words will be verified if they bring Benjamin. Genesis uses the Hebrew אמנ root for words made reliable by a check.

column5: ء م ن / אמנ; table sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary labels iman as confirmation; Genesis uses the Hebrew אמנ root when Jacob does not believe the brothers' true report. The possible cognate appears in the same Yusuf family scene but with truthful news.

column5: ء م ن / אמן; table sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary labels iman as tasdiq; Exodus uses the Hebrew אמן root for Israel's believing in Moses' report after signs. The proposed root correspondence adds a lexical link to the scene's evidence-based belief.

column5: ء م ن / אמנ; table sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The source commentary glosses iman as tasdiq; the Hebrew verb for Israel's belief after seeing the sea uses אמנ. The table's proposed cognate connects the lexical root to a scene of evidence and assent.

column5: ء م ن / אמנ; table sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The source commentary explicitly glosses iman as tasdiq; Genesis uses the Hebrew אמנ root for Abram's belief. The proposed cognate connects the term to a belief that is counted as righteousness.

column5: ء م ن / אמנ; table sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary joins iman to confirmation and haqq to truth; Proverbs uses אמונה for trustworthy speech in contrast to a false witness. The proposed cognate shows the Hebrew root's sense of reliability in testimony.

The commentary describes the far-seeing eye as watching from a distance; Genesis says Abraham lifts his eyes and sees the place from afar. This is a concrete biblical image of distant sight preceding action.
The commentary pairs belief with righteous action; after Abraham does not withhold Isaac, the angel says that now he knows Abraham fears God. The test makes conduct disclose the allegiance professed.

The commentary glosses haqq as correspondence and finding something as it is; the psalm invites its hearers to taste and see that the LORD is good. Sensory testing becomes an image for confirming a claim about God.

The commentary ends its sequence with mutual counsel in patience; Habakkuk says the vision has an appointed time and, even if it seems slow, one must wait for it. Patience is tied to a claim whose fulfillment is awaited.

column5: ء م ن / אמנ; table sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary explains iman as a person's confirming assent; Deuteronomy calls God נאמן, faithful, as covenant keeper to those who love and obey him. The Hebrew root shifts the emphasis from human assent to divine reliability.

column5: ء م ن / אמנ; table sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary quotes Musa's encounter with fire; Numbers calls Moses נאמן, faithful in all God's house. The same proposed root links the figure who sees a sign with a biblical description of reliable service.

column5: ء م ن / Aramaic אמנ; table sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary couples belief with righteous conduct; Biblical Aramaic describes Daniel as מהימן, faithful, when his opponents can find no corruption in him. The root's Aramaic use stresses demonstrated reliability.

column5: ء م ن / אמנ; table sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary defines iman as assent to truth; Habakkuk says the righteous live by אמונה, often rendered faithfulness. The possible cognate preserves a difference between assent and steadfast fidelity.

column5: ء ن س / אנש; BDB-cited Arabic cognate in table
column6: The commentary labels al-insan with ء ن س and develops a seeing human; Job asks whether אנוש, a mortal, can be righteous before God. The cognate possibility adds human frailty to the surah's claim about humanity in loss.

column5: ء ن س / אנש; BDB-cited Arabic cognate in table
column6: The commentary develops al-insan as a human who notices and sees; Job calls אנוש short-lived and full of trouble. The proposed cognate adds the Hebrew Bible's mortal, afflicted sense to the universal human condition in loss.

column5: ع م ل / עמל; table sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary labels righteous deeds with ع م ل and calls the mind's exercise work; Ecclesiastes uses עמל for toil and concludes that the labor brings no gain. The possible root link sets purposeful action against futile toil.

column5: ح ق ق / חקק; table sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary's haqq means truth, conformity, and confirmed rightness; Isaiah condemns people who decree חקק decrees of injustice. The proposed root correspondence warns that something prescribed can still be false or unjust.

column5: ء م ن / Aramaic הימן from אמנ; table correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary labels iman from ء م ن; Onkelos renders Abraham's belief with an Aramaic form from the אמנ family. The table correspondence is only proposed, while the verse gives a Jewish witness to the cognate's use.

column5: Abraham sees a cloud on the mountain
column6: The commentary develops distant sight as perception that can lead to certainty; this midrash reads Abraham's sight of the mountain as seeing a cloud of divine presence, distinguishing his perception from the servants'. It turns seeing into recognition of a sign.

The commentary's exception requires righteous deeds as well as belief; Avot says action is the main thing rather than exposition. The rabbinic maxim gives practice priority in a distinct, concise formulation.

The commentary keeps belief, deeds, truth, and patience together; Makkot's list of prophetic summaries ends with Habakkuk's righteous person living by faithfulness. The rabbis make that one principle a compression of the commandments, a different interpretive emphasis.

column5: mutual reproof in truth and humility
column6: The commentary reads tawasaw bil-haqq as people transmitting confirmed truth to one another; the Community Rule directs members to reprove one another in truth and humility. It makes reciprocal correction a discipline of the community.

The commentary ends with people urging one another to patience; Sirach tells the person serving God to set the heart right and be steadfast in a time of calamity. It makes patient endurance part of faithful service.
The commentary pairs belief with patience; Sirach tells the reader to trust God, hold fast, and hope in him. Its counsel binds trust to endurance.
The commentary's faith and patience stand together; James says the testing of faith produces endurance. It supplies a causal link between belief and sabr.
The commentary closes with counsel to patience; James says endurance must complete its work so believers may be mature. It treats patience as an active process rather than passive delay.
The commentary couples patience with the path out of loss; Paul says suffering produces endurance. This Christian formulation gives hardship a formative relation to sabr.
The commentary's haqq includes confirmation and certainty; Paul says endurance produces tested character, which produces hope. The progression makes endurance itself a proving process.
The commentary pairs righteous action with patience; Hebrews says endurance is needed after doing God's will in order to receive the promise. It binds work, waiting, and fulfillment.
The commentary makes believers part of the exception to loss; Hebrews quotes the righteous living by faith and warns against shrinking back. It links faith with perseverance under pressure.
The commentary pairs iman with deeds; Paul cites Abraham's belief being counted as righteousness. This Christian reading foregrounds credited belief in the same Abraham text.

column5: belief apart from a worker's wage
column6: The commentary's exception explicitly combines belief and deeds; Paul contrasts the worker's wage with the person who believes in the God who justifies the ungodly. This interpretation places emphasis on belief apart from earned payment.

The commentary permits but does not establish a sight-to-belief reading; Hebrews defines faith as assurance concerning hoped-for things and conviction concerning things not seen. It preserves a contrary Christian account of faith's relation to sight.

The commentary says the sequence does not prove that believers must first see; Jesus blesses those who have not seen and yet believe, after Thomas believes on seeing. The verse states the alternative explicitly.
The commentary's proposed reading moves from sight to confirmation but marks it as unproven; Paul says believers walk by faith rather than sight. This preserves a direct contrary formulation.
The commentary reads tawasaw bil-haqq as counsel exchanged among people; the Didache instructs members to reprove one another peacefully. It makes correction reciprocal and governs its manner.

column5: do not tire of doing good
column6: The commentary pairs righteous action with patience; Paul tells the community not to grow weary in doing good. It directly joins sustained action with endurance.
The commentary's tawasaw is mutual counsel; Paul tells the community to admonish an offender as a brother, not treat him as an enemy. The verse supplies a concrete relational form for correction.

The commentary leaves open whether belief follows seeing; Augustine interprets Jesus' blessing of those who believe without seeing as faith's proper condition. This Christian reading sharpens the alternative already stated in John.

The commentary's example of orphan property makes observed sound judgment the trigger for handing over wealth; Avot assigns stages of life to commandments, study, and livelihood. The rabbinic age ladder offers a specific, though not identical, account of recognized maturity.

The commentary says the flat Qur'anic wording does not establish loss as blindness and the exception as sight; Jesus explicitly says he came so the blind may see and the seeing become blind. The Gospel makes that metaphorical reversal explicit.

The commentary's source gloss gives the eye a small visible likeness in its pupil; Paul says present sight is like a dim view in a mirror before face-to-face knowledge. The optical analogy is secondary and the images are not identical.
